blocks.text: In a power-station condenser, exhaust steam from the turbine is turned back into water on cold tubes, releasing about 2.3 MJ for every kilogram. The heat transfer coefficient of that condensation sets the size of a building-sized machine, and surprisingly it depends on how the liquid sits on the metal.

blocks.markdown: When saturated vapour touches a surface colder than $T_{sat}$ it condenses and releases its latent heat. If the liquid **wets** the surface it spreads as a continuous film that drains under gravity: **film condensation**. All the heat must cross this film by conduction, so the film is the main thermal resistance. Its thickness grows from top to bottom of a vertical plate because more condensate accumulates.

blocks.title: Nusselt film condensation
blocks.text: For a vertical plate of height $L$ with a laminar, smooth film, Nusselt's analysis balances gravity against viscous drag in the film and heat conduction across it. It gives the local coefficient $h_x\propto x^{-1/4}$ and the plate average $\bar h_L=\tfrac43h_{x=L}$. The corrected latent heat is $h'_{fg}=h_{fg}+0.68c_{p,l}(T_{sat}-T_s)$ to include subcooling of the condensate.

blocks.caption: Average coefficient, laminar film on a vertical plate or tube; liquid properties at the film temperature (T_sat + T_s)/2, h_fg at T_sat; exact for a wave-free laminar film up to a film Reynolds number of about 30; in the wavy-laminar range (about 30 to 1800) correlations give higher coefficients, so Nusselt theory is conservative there

blocks.title: Steam condensing on a vertical plate
blocks.prompt: Saturated steam at 100 $^\circ$C condenses on a vertical plate 0.5 m high and 1.0 m wide held at 90 $^\circ$C. Use typical properties of the liquid film at about 95 $^\circ$C: $\rho_l=962$ kg/m$^3$, $k_l=0.677$ W/m K, $\mu_l=3.0\times10^{-4}$ Pa s, $c_{p,l}=4210$ J/kg K, with $\rho_v=0.6$ kg/m$^3$ and $h_{fg}=2.257\times10^6$ J/kg. Find the average heat transfer coefficient, the heat rate and the condensation rate, and check that the film is laminar.

steps.text: Corrected latent heat (the condensate is cooled below saturation): $h'_{fg}=h_{fg}+0.68c_{p,l}(T_{sat}-T_s)=2.257\times10^6+0.68\times4210\times10=2.2856e+06$ J/kg.
Nusselt expression: $\bar h_L=0.943\left[\dfrac{g\rho_l(\rho_l-\rho_v)k_l^3h'_{fg}}{\mu_l(T_{sat}-T_s)L}\right]^{1/4}$. The bracket equals $4.2897e+15$, whose fourth root is $8092.95$.
So $\bar h_L=7632$ W/m$^2$K. Heat rate: $q=\bar hA\Delta T=7632\times0.5\times10=38.2$ kW.

Check laminar flow: condensate flow per unit width $\Gamma=0.0167$ kg/m s, and $Re_\delta=4\Gamma/\mu_l=223$. This is above about 30, so the film is wavy-laminar (below about 1800, so not turbulent); Nusselt's result is then a conservative estimate, because waves raise the true coefficient.

blocks.answer: $\bar h_L\approx7632$ W/m$^2$K, $q\approx38$ kW and $\dot m\approx0.017$ kg/s (60 kg/h), with $Re_\delta\approx223$ (wavy-laminar, so the result is conservative).

blocks.markdown: Condensation rate follows from an energy balance. The heat flow through the film is the latent heat released by the condensing vapour, so $q=\dot mh'_{fg}$ and $\dot m=q/h'_{fg}$. The film Reynolds number $Re_\delta=4\Gamma/\mu_l$, with $\Gamma=\dot m/w$ the condensate flow per unit width $w$ at the bottom (kg/m s), indicates whether the laminar assumption holds.

rows: Continuous liquid film on a wetted surface
Discrete droplets that grow, coalesce and roll off
Only the thin region around droplets; most of the surface is bare
Clean, wetted surface; the usual case
Needs non-wetting surface or promoter; hard to sustain
A potential enhancement; designs rarely rely on it
blocks.caption: Film versus dropwise condensation of steam

blocks.markdown: Dropwise condensation gives much higher coefficients because there is no continuous liquid layer to conduct through: droplets grow on bare metal, coalesce and are swept away, which keeps most of the surface exposed to vapour. It requires a surface that is not wetted by the liquid, for example with a thin promoter coating, and the coating wears or the surface fouls, so condensers are normally designed for film condensation as a conservative case.

blocks.title: Condensate flow from the heat removed
blocks.prompt: A steam condenser removes 250 kW from saturated steam at 100 $^\circ$C onto a cooling surface held at 85 $^\circ$C, so $T_{sat}-T_s=15$ K. Find the rate at which steam condenses. Use $h_{fg}=2.257\times10^6$ J/kg and $c_{p,l}=4210$ J/kg K.

steps.text: In steady state all the heat removed comes from condensation of vapour and from cooling the condensate; in the film theory both are included in the corrected latent heat.
Ignoring the subcooling term gives $250000/2.257e+06=0.1108$ kg/s, a difference of 1.9%, so the correction is small for modest $\Delta T$.

blocks.answer: $\dot m\approx0.109$ kg/s (391 kg/h). The subcooling correction changes the answer by only about 1.9%.

items: Evaluate liquid properties at the film temperature and $h_{fg}$ at $T_{sat}$; compute $h'_{fg}$.
Compute $\bar h_L$ with the Nusselt expression.
Check $Re_\delta$ to confirm the laminar assumption.

blocks.title: Do not confuse the temperatures
blocks.text: $\Delta T$ in the Nusselt formula is $T_{sat}-T_s$, the difference across the film. Because $\bar h\propto\Delta T^{-1/4}$, a larger wall subcooling reduces $h$ (thicker film) although the heat rate $q=\bar hA\Delta T\propto\Delta T^{3/4}$ still increases. Liquid properties are at the film temperature, but $h_{fg}$ is at saturation.

blocks.title: Film thickness is the resistance
blocks.text: A thicker film gives a lower coefficient. This is why $\bar h$ decreases with plate height ($\propto L^{-1/4}$), why horizontal tubes (short drainage path) condense better than tall vertical ones, and why dropwise condensation, which has no film, performs much better.

points: Film condensation: $\bar h_L=0.943[g\rho_l(\rho_l-\rho_v)k_l^3h'_{fg}/(\mu_l\Delta TL)]^{1/4}$ with $h'_{fg}=h_{fg}+0.68c_{p,l}\Delta T$ and liquid properties at the film temperature.
Check $Re_\delta=4\Gamma/\mu_l$ for laminar flow; $\bar h\propto\Delta T^{-1/4}L^{-1/4}$.
Dropwise condensation avoids the film resistance and gives much higher coefficients, but is hard to sustain.

questions.stem: Dropwise condensation gives a higher heat transfer coefficient than film condensation mainly because

options.text: the latent heat of the vapour is larger when it condenses as drops
there is no continuous liquid film, so most of the surface is directly exposed to vapour and the film conduction resistance is absent
drops flow faster over the surface than a film does
dropwise condensation occurs at a larger temperature difference

questions.correctOptionText: there is no continuous liquid film, so most of the surface is directly exposed to vapour and the film conduction resistance is absent

distractorRationale.a: $h_{fg}$ is a fluid property and does not depend on the condensate form.
distractorRationale.c: Drop shedding helps but the main effect is removal of the film's thermal resistance.
distractorRationale.d: Dropwise condensation works with the same $\Delta T$; its advantage is a higher $h$ at that $\Delta T$.

questions.explanation: In film condensation all the heat has to be conducted through the liquid layer, whose thickness is the dominant resistance. In dropwise condensation droplets leave bare metal between them, which is directly in contact with vapour, so the coefficient can be 5 to 10 times higher.

questions.stem: For laminar film condensation on a vertical plate, the average heat transfer coefficient $\bar h$ varies with the wall subcooling $\Delta T=T_{sat}-T_s$ as

options.text: $\bar h\propto\Delta T^{-1/4}$, so it decreases as $\Delta T$ increases

questions.correctOptionText: $\bar h\propto\Delta T^{-1/4}$, so it decreases as $\Delta T$ increases

distractorRationale.a: The film gets thicker at larger $\Delta T$ because more condensate forms, so $\bar h$ falls.
distractorRationale.b: The Nusselt expression contains $\Delta T^{-1/4}$ in the denominator.
distractorRationale.d: This would give heat flux proportional to $\Delta T^2$, not the observed $\Delta T^{3/4}$.

questions.explanation: A larger $\Delta T$ condenses more vapour per unit time and thickens the film, which raises its resistance. The heat flux $q''=\bar h\Delta T\propto\Delta T^{3/4}$ still increases with $\Delta T$.

questions.stem: Steam condenses at 75 kW on a cooled surface. Taking the latent heat as $h_{fg}=2.257\times10^6$ J/kg and ignoring the subcooling correction, find the condensation rate in kg/s.
questions.explanation: The condensation rate is $\dot m=q/h_{fg}=75000/2.257e+06=0.0332$ kg/s, or 120 kg/h. Almost all the heat comes from the latent heat of vaporisation.

questions.stem: Saturated steam at 100 $^\circ$C condenses on a vertical plate 1.2 m high held at 95 $^\circ$C. Use film properties $\rho_l=960$ kg/m$^3$, $k_l=0.678$ W/m K, $\mu_l=2.9\times10^{-4}$ Pa s, $c_{p,l}=4210$ J/kg K, $\rho_v=0.6$ kg/m$^3$ and $h_{fg}=2.257\times10^6$ J/kg. Use the Nusselt expression with $h'_{fg}$. Find the average heat transfer coefficient in W/m$^2$K.
questions.explanation: $h'_{fg}=2.257\times10^6+0.68\times4210\times5=2.2713e+06$ J/kg. The bracket is $g\rho_l(\rho_l-\rho_v)k_l^3h'_{fg}/(\mu_l\Delta TL)=3.676e+15$, with fourth root 7786.45. Then $\bar h_L=0.943\times$ that $=7343$ W/m$^2$K.

questions.stem: A vertical plate of area 0.6 m$^2$ is at 12 K below the saturation temperature of the steam condensing on it, with an average coefficient of 6200 W/m$^2$K. The corrected latent heat is $h'_{fg}=2.30\times10^6$ J/kg. Find the condensation rate in kg/h.
questions.explanation: Heat rate: $q=\bar hA\Delta T=6200\times0.6\times12=44.6$ kW. Condensation rate $\dot m=q/h'_{fg}=44640/2.30e+06=0.01941$ kg/s $=69.9$ kg/h.

questions.stem: A vertical condensing plate has its height doubled while the wall temperature, fluid and film regime stay the same. The average heat transfer coefficient is multiplied by about

distractorRationale.b: This would need $\bar h\propto L^{-1}$; the film correlation has $L^{-1/4}$.
distractorRationale.c: This is $2^{1/4}$; the average coefficient decreases with plate height.
distractorRationale.d: The thicker film on a taller plate lowers the coefficient, so it is not independent of height.

questions.explanation: $\bar h\propto L^{-1/4}$ so doubling $L$ gives $2^{-1/4}=0.841$. The extra length lets the condensate film thicken, which raises resistance on the lower part of the plate.

questions.stem: In the Nusselt analysis the effective latent heat is $h'_{fg}=h_{fg}+0.68c_{p,l}(T_{sat}-T_s)$ because

options.text: the vapour is superheated and loses sensible heat
the film conducts additional heat axially
the latent heat increases with the plate height
the condensate is cooled below the saturation temperature, releasing extra sensible heat

questions.correctOptionText: the condensate is cooled below the saturation temperature, releasing extra sensible heat

distractorRationale.a: The theory is for saturated vapour, not superheated.
distractorRationale.b: Axial conduction is neglected in the analysis.
distractorRationale.c: $h_{fg}$ is a property of the fluid at saturation, independent of geometry.

questions.explanation: In the film, the temperature varies from $T_{sat}$ at the vapour interface to $T_s$ at the wall, so the condensate gives up some sensible heat as it cools. The factor 0.68 is a standard refinement for the temperature profile in the film, and the term is a small correction for modest $\Delta T$.

questions.stem: Explain why dropwise condensation gives a higher heat transfer coefficient than film condensation. Why are industrial condensers normally designed on the basis of film condensation?
markingGuide: In film condensation heat must be conducted through the continuous liquid layer, so its thickness sets the main thermal resistance.
In dropwise condensation drops form on the bare surface, grow, coalesce and roll off, exposing fresh metal, so there is no continuous resistance and $h$ is 5 to 10 times higher.
Dropwise condensation needs a non-wetting surface or a promoter, which wears, oxidises or fouls and cannot be relied on over the plant life.
Film condensation gives a conservative, reliable design basis; dropwise gains are treated as a bonus.
questions.explanation: The answer rests on the thermal resistance of the liquid layer. The design practice follows from risk: a design that works for film condensation also works if dropwise condensation is lost.

questions.stem: The local coefficient in laminar film condensation on a vertical plate varies as $h_x\propto x^{-1/4}$, where $x$ is the distance down from the top. Show that the plate average is $\bar h_L=\tfrac43h_{x=L}$, and explain physically why $h_x$ falls as $x$ increases.
markingGuide: The film is thin at the top and thickens downward as condensate accumulates, so conduction resistance $\delta/k_l$ increases with $x$ and $h_x=k_l/\delta$ falls.
The thin film near the top has large $h$, which raises the average above the value at the bottom.
questions.explanation: The integral of $x^{-1/4}$ gives a factor of $4/3$. The physics is that film thickness grows with accumulated condensate, so $\delta\propto x^{1/4}$ and $h_x=k/\delta$ falls as $x^{-1/4}$.

questions.stem: Saturated steam at 100 $^\circ$C condenses on a vertical plate 0.8 m high and 0.4 m wide held at 92 $^\circ$C. Use the film properties $\rho_l=962$ kg/m$^3$, $k_l=0.677$ W/m K, $\mu_l=3.0\times10^{-4}$ Pa s, $c_{p,l}=4210$ J/kg K, $\rho_v=0.6$ kg/m$^3$, $h_{fg}=2.257\times10^6$ J/kg. Find the condensation rate in kg/h and check the film regime ($Re_\delta<1800$ means laminar, possibly wavy).
questions.explanation: $h'_{fg}=2.2799e+06$ J/kg. $\bar h_L=0.943[\ldots]^{1/4}=7170$ W/m$^2$K. Heat rate $q=7170\times(0.8\times0.4)\times8=18.36$ kW. Then $\dot m=q/h'_{fg}=0.00805$ kg/s $=29.0$ kg/h. Check: $\Gamma=\dot m/w=0.0201$ kg/m s, so $Re_\delta=4\Gamma/\mu_l=268<1800$, which is wavy-laminar (above about 30), so the Nusselt value is a conservative estimate.
